insight.title: Why City Streets Are Often Angled at 45 Degrees
insight.subtitle: A centuries-old desire for sunlight and airflow still dictates the orientation of our modern neighborhoods.

sections.text: When you walk through grid-patterned cities like New York or Chicago, you’ll notice many blocks aren’t perfectly aligned north-to-south. Instead, they tilt at an angle, skewing the city’s footprint against the compass.

This wasn't an accident or a surveyor’s mistake. Architects in the 19th century intentionally angled street grids to ensure that sunlight could reach the lower floors of buildings, preventing the "canyon effect" of permanent shadows.

By tilting the grid, city planners maximized the hours of direct solar exposure on both sides of the street. This subtle geometry remains the reason your apartment gets light at specific times each day.
The sun doesn't follow the grid, so the grid followed the sun.
